Crew Dispatch and Route Optimization

CivicOps AI · genetic algorithm for rank-aware crew assignment, A* routing on the NYC road network, rolling-horizon replanning. Research prototype; proposals only.

SummaryData and designMethodValidationStatic resultsDynamic resultsSensitivity and checksDemonstrationsLimitationsReproduce

1. Summary

This component turns the C11 prioritised queue into a proposed crew dispatch plan: which requests are assigned, to which crew, in what order and along which roads, with estimated times, and why every other request waits. A genetic algorithm (evolutionary computing) assigns and sequences jobs; A* search (informed search) on a locally enriched OpenStreetMap network provides road-following routes and travel times. The only priority input is C11's overall_queue_position; nothing here authorises dispatch.

Honest headline. The GA clearly beats serving requests strictly in rank order (more served, far less travel). Against the travel-efficient greedy baseline it serves about the same number but travels 2–10% more; its advantage there is that it keeps C11's rank order almost intact, whereas that baseline bypasses higher-ranked requests about 87–100 times per episode. All results are simulations on real request locations and arrival times, the real road network and synthetic crews.

2. Data and evaluation design

Inputs and their nature

  • observed NYC311 historical extract: 49,558 requests in 296 replay episodes (sampled ~2-hour borough windows); after-the-fact columns never copied (9 excluded).
  • observed OSM drive network: 59,251 nodes, 149,355 directed edges (© OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL).
  • imputed edge speeds: 29.4% from OSM tags, 63.1% NYC 25 mph default, 7.4% road-class median, 0.07% fallback.
  • synthetic crew rosters sized from the train split at capacity factors 0.6/0.8/1.0/1.2 (91, 113, 139, 162 crews) plus the original legacy roster (136).
  • simulated approvals, Crew Portal status updates, durations and breakdowns in the dynamic replay (labelled in every event).

Time-based split (project rule)

splitepisodesused for
train202workforce sizing only
val44objective and GA-size selection

Validation selection used a rule written before the sweep; one documented amendment extended the λB grid because the optimum sat on its boundary (§4). Test episodes were untouched until the configuration was frozen. Paired comparisons per episode: Wilcoxon signed-rank, 95% bootstrap CI, Holm correction.

3. Method in brief

Optimisation (GA)

  • One sub-problem per agency (exact, since agency is a hard constraint).
  • Chromosome: an ordered stop list per crew plus an unserved pool. Every operator keeps plans feasible: skills, agency, work-time budget including the return to depot, no duplicates, locked work untouched.
  • Route-based crossover; relocate, exchange, 2-opt, ruin-and-recreate and swap-in mutations; tournament selection with elitism.
  • Objective (frozen after validation): lexicographic, i.e. first minimise the rank-weighted backlog (weights w(r) = 1/log2(r+1) from overall_queue_position), then travel, rank-weighted start delay and plan changes.

Routing (A*) and dynamics

  • Edge cost = length / (posted speed × 0.6); the factor is an uncalibrated assumption tested from 0.5 to 1.0.
  • Heuristics: straight-line distance / top speed (admissible: every edge is at least as long as the straight line, checked on all 148,904 edges) and ALT landmarks; both exact against Dijkstra.
  • The GA reads a cached travel-time matrix; A* reconstructs the final road-following legs.
  • Rolling horizon: event-driven controller, commit at departure, change penalty and publish threshold for stability; agency operating hours (07:00–19:00, NYPD 24 h) with night requests planned at opening.

4. Validation: choosing the objective

Low λB makes the GA skip far-away requests: at λB = 60 it serves fewer requests than rank-first greedy. The selected objective serves 104.7 requests per validation episode with 0.00 avoidable inversions per 100 served and 9.2 travel minutes per served request (rank-first greedy: 88.9 / 0.00 / 17.0; travel-aware greedy: 103.7 / 74.3 / 8.9). GA size "small" was within 0.33% of the best at 1.9 s mean run time.

  • Rolling GA vs a static GA plan with insertion only: travel -72 min (pHolm = 3e-06); completed +1.4 (pHolm = 0.24, not significant); at the cost of more reassignments (51 vs 6 per episode).
  • Stability mechanism: without it, reassignments rise from 51 to 96 per episode (pHolm = 0.0002) with no detectable quality gain.
  • Rolling GA vs rolling rank-first greedy: completed +9.7, travel -429 min, but high-ranked requests start 7.2 min later on average (a negative result).
  • Locked-commitment violations: 0 in all 392 runs.

8. Demonstrations on real data

D1 · Static proposal (Manhattan test window, 162 eligible requests)

138 requests planned, rank-weighted coverage 0.86. Routes follow the road graph; numbers give the planned order.

D2 · Crew shortage and backlog (same window)

Capacity 0.6 (17 crews): 96 planned, coverage 0.65. Capacity 1.2 (28 crews): 144 planned, coverage 0.89. Unserved reasons: CAPACITY_USED_BY_OTHER_REQUESTS 65, NO_COMPATIBLE_CREW 1 (capacity 0.6).

D3 · Dynamic replay (Staten Island test window, 68 real arrivals)

51 jobs completed in simulation, 36 plan versions, 0 locked-commitment violations. Review/hold flags and all execution events are simulated and labelled.

Also in this run: a cancellation (plan_v0008.json) and a human-review completion that makes a request eligible (plan_v0011.json). Plans: outputs/demos/D3_dynamic_replay/plans/; audit log: events/events.jsonl.

D4 · Night window and operating hours

Window starting 2026-09-11 00:03: NYPD (24 h) plans immediately; the other agencies' crews are on duty 07:00–19:00, so their work is planned for the opening. 70 of 75 completed in simulation.

9. Limitations

  • No real dispatch ground truth (crew, order, travel or on-site times); all results are simulations.
  • Crews are synthetic; capacity factors are relative to the demand of sampled windows, not NYC staffing.
  • The full c11_final (with C10 and the official SLA tables) was not runnable here; the replay used the vendored, unmodified c11_prioritization.py with the catalog's default urgency as the C10 input. Dispatch uses only the returned positions.
  • Travel speeds are posted limits scaled by an uncalibrated factor; no turn penalties or live traffic.
  • Episodes are independent 2-hour windows with no carried-over backlog; one borough's crews per episode.
  • Approvals are simulated at departure; real approval latency is not modelled. No GPU path (not needed at this scale).

Full list: research/limitations.md; assumptions with their status: research/assumptions.md.

10. Reproducing these results

python -m crew_dispatch experiment tuning        # validation (+ tuning_ext, amendment A1)
python -m crew_dispatch experiment all           # routing, exact gap, static, speed, budget, dynamic (test)
python -c "from crew_dispatch.research.analysis import analyze_all; analyze_all()"
python -m crew_dispatch demo
python scripts/build_report.py                   # regenerates this file
